extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors studying real analysis/advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and criteria from a real-analysis textbook on continuity, interchange of limits, uniform convergence, equicontinuity (Ascoli), interchange of derivative and limit, and basic Riemann integration. Presents definitions, theorems, proofs, examples, and tests used to decide when limits/interchanges/integrals are valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains extrema (Theorem 1.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: A continuous function f from a closed bounded interval [a,b] into R is bounded and takes on maximum and minimum values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Bolzano–Weierstrass: choose sequence approaching sup, extract convergent subsequence, use continuity to show limit point attains the sup. (Symmetric argument for minimum.) This is the standard extreme value theorem and is used as a tool in later proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate Value Theorem (Theorem 1.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : [a,b] → R is continuous, then f on [a,b] takes on all values between f(a) and f(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof presented via a Bolzano–Weierstrass style argument; remark notes a conceptually clearer proof will highlight that the essential property is the connectedness of [a,b]. The proof constructs sets A and B of points mapping below/above a target value and uses supremum/infimum and subsequence arguments; contradictions are used to force the desired value to be attained. Useful warning: pointwise convergence of continuous functions need not preserve continuity—uniform convergence is the right hypothesis for preserving continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated limits need not commute (illustrative examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general lim_i lim_j b_{ij} need not equal lim_j lim_i b_{ij}; examples show two iterated limits can differ (e.g., an infinite matrix with 1's above diagonal, 0's below).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative analytic examples (sequences of functions, series) demonstrate where interchanging limits fails. Takeaway: without extra hypotheses (monotonicity, uniformity, etc.) one cannot interchange iterated limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone doubly-indexed sequences: equality of iterated limits (Theorem 1.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let b_{ij} ∈ R* be ≥ 0 and monotone increasing in i for each j and in j for each i. Then iterated limits and the joint limit exist and coincide: lim_j lim_i b_{ij} = lim_i lim_j b_{ij} = lim_{i,j→∞} b_{ij}, with all indicated limits existing in R*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: use monotonicity to compare row and column limits, derive contradictions if unequal. Pictorially, monotonicity forces the far-down-right entries to be close to the same value. This result underlies monotone convergence phenomena and has corollaries for sums/products; it foreshadows measure-theoretic monotone convergence and Fubini theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-sum corollary for monotone sequences (Corollary 1.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_{lj} ∈ R* are ≥ 0 and are monotone increasing in j for each l, then the iterated sums satisfy Σ_l (Σ_j a_{lj}) = Σ_j (Σ_l a_{lj}), with the limits existing in R*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Theorem 1.13 by setting b_{ij} = Σ_{l=1}^i a_{lj}. This gives a practical criterion for interchanging order of summation under monotone nonnegativity hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product/sum corollary for nonnegative terms (Corollary 1.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If c_{ij} ∈ R* are ≥ 0 for all i,j, then double sums/products can be interchanged: Σ_i (Σ_j c_{ij}) = Σ_j (Σ_i c_{ij}), with the limits existing in R*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from Corollary 1.14. This is the discrete analogue of Fubini/Tonelli style results under nonnegativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of uniform convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence f_n of functions on a nonempty set S converges uniformly to f on S if for every ε>0 there exists N such that for all n ≥ N and all x∈S, |f_n(x) - f(x)| ≤ ε. Equivalently sup_x |f_n(x)-f(x)| → 0 as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is central: uniform convergence gives estimates independent of the parameter x and is what allows interchange of limits with continuity, integration, differentiation (under additional hypotheses). Many subsequent propositions test or use uniform convergence via sup-norm or Cauchy-type criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1.16: interchange criteria using uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Let b_{ij} be real numbers with lim_j b_{ij} existing uniformly in i and lim_i b_{ij} existing for each j. Then various conclusions follow: (a) if lim_i L_i exists then it equals lim_j L'_j; (b) lim_j L'_j exists; (c) equality of the two iterated limits; (d) double limit exists and equals the iterated limits if lim_i L_i exists; (e) lim_j L'_j = lim_i (lim_j b_{ij}) when lim_i b_{ij} exists uniformly in j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposition is a prototype for many limit-interchange results: uniform convergence in one index together with existence of limits in the other index forces equality of iterated limits and often the existence of the double limit. The proof uses ε-arguments, choosing indices from the uniform hypothesis to control the matrix entries. The statement enumerates (a)-(e) as alternative extra conclusions available in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform Cauchy criterion (Proposition 1.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of functions on S is uniformly Cauchy (for every ε>0 exists N such that for n,m ≥ N and all x∈S, |f_n(x)-f_m(x)| ≤ ε) if and only if it converges uniformly on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof mirrors the usual Cauchy → completeness argument applied pointwise plus a uniform 2ε trick to upgrade to uniform convergence. This criterion is useful when explicit limit functions are unknown but Cauchy estimates are accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform alternating-series (Leibniz) test for functions (Corollary 1.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for each x in S the sequence a_n(x) is monotone decreasing, nonnegative, and lim_n a_n(x)=0 uniformly in x, then the alternating series Σ (-1)^n a_n(x) converges uniformly on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the uniform Cauchy criterion to the sequence of partial sums; the monotone alternating structure yields uniform small tails when a_n → 0 uniformly. This is the uniform analogue of the Leibniz test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summation-by-parts uniform convergence criterion (Corollary 1.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a_n(x) is a sequence of nonnegative functions, monotone in n and tending to 0 uniformly in x, and if B_n(x)=Σ_{k=1}^n b_k(x) have partial sums bounded by some M uniformly in n and x, then Σ a_n(x) b_n(x) converges uniformly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses summation by parts and uniform Cauchy control: choose N so that a_k small uniformly for k≥N, then bound tails via the uniform bound M. This generalizes the alternating-series-type tests and is convenient when multiplicative factors have bounded partial sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass M-test (Proposition 1.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If for functions f_n on S there exist constants M_n with |f_n(x)| ≤ M_n for all x∈S and Σ M_n < ∞, then Σ f_n(x) converges uniformly on S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard test: reduce to uniform Cauchy by tail control via Σ_{k=n+1}^m M_k → 0. Useful as an easy-to-apply sufficient condition for uniform convergence of series of functions (absolute convergence uniformly). Examples show M-test may not apply in all uniformly convergent cases, but when it does it is simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous (Theorem 1.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If each f_n is continuous at x and f_n → f uniformly, then f is continuous at x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequality and the uniform control to make each of three terms small (a 3ε argument). In practice, if each f_n is continuous on [a,b] and convergence is uniform on [a,b], f is continuous on [a,b]. This is a principal application of uniform convergence (exchanging limit and continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform near-x control from uniform convergence (Theorem 1.210)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f_n are continuous at x and f_n → f uniformly, then for each ε>0 there exist N and δ>0 such that for all n ≥ N and all t with |t-x|<δ, |f(t)-f(x) - (f_n(t)-f_n(x))| < ε (equivalently simultaneous control of approximants and continuity near x for all large n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strengthened local estimate combining uniform convergence and pointwise continuity; proof picks N from uniform convergence and δ from continuity of a chosen approximant f_N. It provides the quantitative uniformity needed in some limit-interchange arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equicontinuity and Ascoli's Theorem (Theorem 1.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: a family F of real-valued functions on [a,b] is equicontinuous at x if ∀ε>0 ∃δ>0 s.t. |t-x|<δ ⇒ |f(t)-f(x)|<ε for all f∈F; uniformly equicontinuous if δ can be chosen independent of x. Theorem (Ascoli): If {f_n} is equicontinuous at each point of [a,b] and pointwise bounded on [a,b], then (a) the family is uniformly equicontinuous and uniformly bounded on [a,b], and (b) {f_n} has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Bolzano–Weierstrass, diagonalization (Cantor diagonal process) to get a subsequence convergent on rationals and then uniform equicontinuity to extend to all points and obtain uniform Cauchy property. Example: family with bounded derivatives yields equicontinuity by Mean Value Theorem. Counterexample: unbounded constants show necessity of boundedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange of derivative and limit (Theorem 1.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose f_n are differentiable on (a,b) with f_n' converging uniformly on (a,b) and suppose f_n(x_0) converges for some x_0 ∈ [a,b]. If f_n converge (pointwise) to f, then for a<x<b we have f'(x)=lim_n f_n'(x); i.e., the derivative and the limit can be interchanged and the derivative limit exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: use Mean Value Theorem to express differences of f_n-f_m via derivatives at intermediate points, obtain uniform Cauchy property of the sequence of difference quotients (ϕ_n), show ϕ_n converge uniformly to a continuous limit using Theorem 1.21, and identify that limit with f'. Uniform convergence of derivatives is essential (counterexamples exist if it is dropped, e.g., sin(nx)/n-type pathologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and criterion for Riemann integrability (partition, upper/lower sums)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounded f:[a,b]→R, partition P: a=x_0 ≤ x_1 ≤ ... ≤ x_n=b. Define M_i = sup_{x∈[x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x), m_i = inf_{[x_{i-1},x_i]} f(x), U(P,f)=Σ M_i Δx_i, L(P,f)=Σ m_i Δx_i. Upper and lower integrals are inf_P U(P,f) and sup_P L(P,f). f is Riemann integrable iff these two numbers coincide; the common value is ∫_a^b f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions include mesh(P)=max Δx_i and allow repeated partition points (zero-length subintervals). Visual interpretation: upper sums approximate area by rectangles above graph; lower sums by rectangles below. This serves as the basic evaluative standard for Riemann integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples for Riemann integrability (continuous/constant vs. everywhere-discontinuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant functions are integrable with obvious sums; Dirichlet function (1 on rationals, 0 on irrationals) is discontinuous everywhere and not Riemann integrable because every partition yields U(P,f)=b-a and L(P,f)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate necessity of some regularity (continuity almost-everywhere or finiteness of discontinuities) for Riemann integrability; they motivate later theorems proving that bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities are integrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds for integrals via global bounds (Lemma 1.24)
rubrics_metrics.description: If m ≤ f(x) ≤ M on [a,b], then for every partition P, m(b-a) ≤ L(P,f) ≤ ∫_a^b f ≤ U(P,f) ≤ M(b-a); taking suprema/infima gives m(b-a) ≤ lower integral ≤ upper integral ≤ M(b-a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple inequality useful for quick estimates and to show integrals lie between bounds; often used to bound errors and for comparison arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity and refinement properties of Riemann sums; integrability criterion by oscillation (Lemma 1.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P* refines P then L(P,f) ≤ L(P*,f) and U(P*,f) ≤ U(P,f). For any two partitions P1,P2, L(P1,f) ≤ U(P2,f). The lower integral is ≤ upper integral. f is Riemann integrable iff for each ε>0 there exists a partition P with U(P,f) - L(P,f) < ε (i.e., upper and lower sums can be made arbitrarily close).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard technical facts about upper/lower sums used to prove integrability and manipulate partitions. The refinement monotonicity and the ε-criterion are the operative check used to show specific functions are Riemann integrable.
